where: Results, freezing thresholds (Experiment 3); Materials and methods
quote: The behavioral thresholds of intact beetles (mean ± SEM) were 0.41 ± 0.08 m/s2 at 20 Hz, 0.33 ± 0.06 m/s2 at 100 Hz, and 0.27 ± 0.06 m/s2 at l kHz (n = 8–18).
note: The page prints '1 kHz' as 'l kHz' in this sentence. The threshold method followed Experiment 1, where each beetle was tested repeatedly with random frequency order and intervals over a minute; whether the freezing groups were tested once or repeatedly is not stated. After the femoral chordotonal organ was operated on, freezing at 100 Hz and 1 kHz dropped to 9.5 % and 0 % of beetles, so the organ is implicated for freezing at those frequencies, not shown for every response. Walking from a standstill was evoked at 0.03 m/s2, but the authors call that threshold unclear. Name: GBIF species match ACCEPTED (Cerambycidae).

source.authors: Pereira AC, Aguilera P, Caputi AA
source.title: The active electrosensory range of Gymnotus omarorum

where: Discussion, section 'Behavioral evidence for short detection range and the decay of location precision'
quote: Behavioral estimation of the active electrolocation range was on average less than one-fifth of the fish's total length and never surpassed one-third for any of the experiments reported in this study.
note: A distance-of-response measure, not a receptor threshold: the authors say the stimulus-field limit depends on receptor threshold. Distances were measured from the closest point of the object, so they are underestimated for longer objects. Probes were small (6 x 12 mm and 8 x 20 mm cylinders) and the fish were restrained with a straight body. Locating a small object decays faster with distance than detecting it (response lost beyond about 10 mm in the discrimination test). Name: GBIF species match ACCEPTED (Gymnotidae, Gymnotiformes). Elsewhere the Discussion says the detection range is, at the most, three object lengths.

method: rectangular bipolar pulsed current at 45 Hz, 0.3 ms pulse width, 3 s stimuli; any visible change in behaviour scored as a response; thresholds from a modified staircase with Bayesian modelling and ROC cut-off

note: The catshark threshold was significantly higher than seabass (P_MCMC = 0.001) and common sole (P_MCMC = 0.001). Electroreceptive species were not more sensitive than the non-electroreceptive ones (electroreceptive against non-electroreceptive, P_MCMC = 0.332); the authors suggest the 45 Hz, 0.3 ms pulse puts most of its energy at frequencies above the receptors' range, and say a receptor response at high frequency does not necessarily evoke a behavioural response. Pulse-trawl field, not a low-frequency prey-like field; length range within species was limited. Crossref year 2024 (volume 10).
